Q: Parsing of postgresql query plans A:

The delay is not "waiting" for the last tuple; it is the CPU time spent calculating the aggregates for 3 million rows.

You are observing a gap between the Bitmap Heap Scan (~4s) and the HashAggregate (~19s). The difference (~15s) is the exclusive execution time of the HashAggregate node itself.

Here is what is actually happening during that 15-second gap:

1. Heavy Per-Row Computation

Your query is aggregating approximately 2.99 million rows (as seen in rows=2990485 1). For every single one of those 3 million rows, the HashAggregate node must:

  • Evaluate the expressions (e.g., l_extendedprice * (1 - discount) 2).

  • Update the internal state for all 8 aggregate functions (sums, avgs, counts) 3.

Even though the Bitmap Heap Scan hands over the rows quickly (within 4 seconds), the HashAggregate has to do significant math on each one.

  • $15,000 \text{ ms} / 3,000,000 \text{ rows} \approx 0.005 \text{ ms per row}$.

  • 5 microseconds per row to update 8 different aggregates and calculate complex expressions is very reasonable behavior for the CPU.

2. Pipelining, Not Waiting

You asked: "When Bitmap Heap Scan... outputs the last tuple, my HashAggregate should have processed the previous tuple."

This is correct. The HashAggregate processes rows as they stream in from the scan. The timer you see on the HashAggregate node starts when the query starts and ends when the final result is ready. It doesn't "wait" at the end; it has simply been busy working the CPU at 100% load during that entire window to process the stream.

3. agg_retrieve_hash_table is Instant

You suspected the function agg_retrieve_hash_table (which projects the final results) might be slow.

  • This is incorrect.

  • Your plan shows rows=6 4and Batches: 1 Memory Usage: 32kB5.

  • Finalizing the hash table only involves iterating over those 6 groups. This takes microseconds, effectively 0 time.

Q: Eclipse IDE highlights a correct C++ function with "Invalid arguments. Candidates are...' A:

Dear future Eclipse/Zed/Vim user,

The problem is this: without intellisense, the opensource editors use language servers, which run in parallel to code execution and analyze code. They do NOT have information on all the files/libraries you use, and without context analyze all the files, even if they're linked, as if they were separate. To remedy the problem, you need to pass the actual build instructions into the analyzer.

Specifically for c++ a lot of editors use clangd, and Eclipse just doesn't telegraph that it needs any additional setup(except the decription of CDT-LSP). It needs something called compile_commands.json, which links all the context needed to analyze every individual files(which is why example code you might ask for will contain a lot of repetitive library additions). Fortunately, Clangd has a stellar tutorial, and LLMs are generally good at generating templates. Even more fortunately, Cmake can generate the compile_commands.json on it's own.

As @user4581301 suggested, to make CMake generate commands you just need to add a flag via set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS 1).

Your job is to change CompilationDatabase parameter in .clangd config file to the location inside your cmake ./build/... folder where it will search for compile_commands.json Cmake just generated. You will, obviously, need to build the program beforehand, so you still need to write correct code at least for the first time.

Voila. Problem gone.

Q: Extra class prediction result shown when testing on AlexeyAB Yolov4 Darknet package on Colab A:

This is normal behaviour.

You are "always" going to get a lot of detections. But you can also see that some of your detections are below the 50% confidence score. Which should be discarded.

I think the pipeline already performs Non-maximum suppression (NMS) to remove duplicates and overlapping detections (not sure), but you can additionally set up confidence score threshold as well, to show only above 50% with -thresh 0.5

This will give you final expected results. Still, if you continue to obtain more than you should, well, this is the goal of everyone :)

It's all about hyperparameter tuning and more data to train our models to give our desired outcome.
